name: FoundationDB
summary: A distributed ordered key-value database whose native API exposes optimistic ACID transactions, read versions, atomic mutations, and a layered implementation with independently evolving data services.

features.name: Ordered key-value transaction API
features.description: FoundationDB presents an ordered key-value store through language bindings and performs reads and writes through transactions, including range reads and atomic operations.
benefits: Provides a small stable substrate for higher-level data models
Makes ordering and transactional boundaries available to client layers
costs: Applications must encode higher-level schemas and indexes
Transaction size, conflicts, and retry behavior constrain workloads

features.name: Optimistic versioned ACID transactions
features.description: The native transaction API exposes read versions, commit, conflict-aware retries, snapshot reads, and atomic operations; the transaction model uses versions to determine read and commit boundaries.
benefits: Provides serializable transaction semantics as a storage primitive
Allows clients to retry conflicts without implementing distributed locking
costs: Contention can cause retries or transaction failure
Read and write conflict ranges make transaction shape an operational concern

features.name: Layered database services
features.description: FoundationDB documents a layered architecture in which a transactional key-value core is complemented by services such as data distribution, storage, transaction processing, and higher-level layers.
benefits: Separates core correctness from specialized data-model services
Allows layers to add indexes or records without changing the transactional substrate
costs: Cross-layer behavior and failure recovery require explicit contracts
The core key-value interface leaves schema and query work to layers

features.name: Distributed replication and recovery path
features.description: The official architecture documentation describes transaction processing, storage servers, data distribution, replication, and recovery as cooperating cluster roles around the ordered key-value transaction boundary.
benefits: Spreads storage and transaction work across commodity-server clusters
Supports recovery and re-replication as cluster membership or failures change
costs: Network coordination and replicated state add latency and operational complexity
Availability and performance depend on deployment topology and failure mode

mathematical_views.question: Under what read-version, conflict-range, and commit-version conditions can a transaction be committed without violating serializability?
assumptions: Keys and ranges are the observable state space
The transaction system validates conflicts before assigning a successful commit version
Client retry is modeled as a new transaction attempt

mathematical_views.question: Which higher-level records and indexes can refine to ordered key-value transactions while preserving their stated API invariants?
assumptions: Each layer declares its key encoding and transaction usage
The core transaction contract is preserved across layer implementation changes
Query performance is treated separately from semantic refinement

mathematical_views.question: How do transaction processing, data distribution, storage, and recovery transitions preserve key-value state across failures?
assumptions: Cluster roles and replication policies are explicit state variables
The model distinguishes committed versions from durable replica placement
Failure and recovery traces are bounded by the documented architecture

benefits: Stable primitive for multiple data models
costs: Schema, indexing, and query semantics move to clients or layers

benefits: Strong transactional contract without application locks
costs: Conflict retries and transaction limits affect tail latency

benefits: Composable separation between core and data models
costs: Layer contracts and operational dependencies add complexity
Network, replica, and topology coordination costs
